english.quote: For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of the deceitful are opened against me: they have spoken against me with a lying tongue.
For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer.
And they have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love.
Set thou a wicked man over him: and let Satan stand at his right hand.
When he shall be judged, let him be condemned: and let his prayer become sin.
Let his days be few; and let another take his office.
Because that he remembered not to shew mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, that he might even slay the broken in heart.
As he loved cursing, so let it come unto him: as he delighted not in blessing, so let it be far from him.
As he clothed himself with cursing like as with his garment, so let it come into his bowels like water, and like oil into his bones.
Let it be unto him as the garment which covereth him, and for a girdle wherewith he is girded continually.
Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the Lord, and of them that speak evil against my soul.
But do thou for me, O God the Lord, for thy name's sake: because thy mercy is good, deliver thou me.

overlap.title: Satan “came also among them” — is he one of the sons of God, and by what standing does he come before the Lord?
overlap.summary: Twice Satan comes before the Lord with the sons of God, is questioned, and is given power over Job within limits. The passage does not say whether he is one of the sons of God, what his office is, or why he is admitted.
overlap.reasoning: The verses quoted state what Satan does: he comes on the day the sons of God come, says he has been going to and fro in the earth, challenges the Lord about Job, is twice given leave with a limit, and goes out from the presence of the Lord. They do not state what he is. “Among them” can be read as one of their number or as one who came in beside them; “also” can be read either way. The matter bears on how the whole account is read: whether Job’s losses come from a servant of the heavenly court doing a task, or from an enemy of God who is allowed to act.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that Satan is here one of the sons of God whose part is to accuse or test; that he is an adversary of God who comes in uninvited or by permission; and that the word is a title for an office, not a name. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV, the Hebrew or the Greek quoted, and this record asserts none. The Greek word differs from the KJV’s name, and the Greek of 1:6 calls the others angels; neither says whether he is one of them. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV Old Testament was searched for the word “Satan” outside Job (four verses: 1 Chronicles 21:1; Psalms 109:6; Zechariah 3:1 and 3:2) and all four were read; Revelation 12:9–10 was read as well. Zechariah shows Satan standing to resist a man before the angel of the Lord and being rebuked, and Revelation speaks of an accuser before God who is cast down; neither says what his standing was in the scene of Job 1 and 2. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. The Hebrew and Greek of the verses outside Job were not compared. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

english.quote: The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
The Lord shall send the rod of thy strength out of Zion: rule thou in the midst of thine enemies.
The Lord hath sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.
He saith unto them, How then doth David in spirit call him Lord, saying,

Until I make thy foes thy footstool.

overlap.title: Who was Melchizedek, and how did he come to be priest of the most high God?
overlap.summary: Melchizedek appears for three verses as king of Salem and priest of the most high God, blesses Abram and receives a tenth, and is not mentioned again in Genesis. His people, his descent and how he came to be a priest are not stated.
overlap.reasoning: Genesis 14:18 is the first verse in the packaged KJV that contains the word “priest”. Melchizedek is introduced without parents, people or history; he is a king of a city in the land where Abram is a stranger, and he is priest of the God whom Abram in verse 22 names as the Lord. Abram accepts his blessing and a tenth is given. The passage does not say how a king of Salem came to serve that God, who made him a priest, or what became of him.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is taken up elsewhere but, on the check made, not answered. Hebrews 7:3 remarks on exactly this: “Without father, without mother, without descent”. Readers take that either as a statement about the man himself or as a statement about what the record leaves out; Hebrews does not say which, and it gives him no people or lineage. Psalms 110:4 speaks of an “order of Melchizedek” without describing how it began. That Salem is Jerusalem is drawn by readers from Psalms 76:2; Genesis does not say so. That he was a human priest-king, or an appearance of a heavenly figure, are both interpretations; the passage states neither, and this record asserts neither. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV containing “Melchizedek” or “Melchisedec” was read (11 verses: Genesis 14:18; Psalms 110:4; Hebrews 5:6, 5:10, 6:20, 7:1, 7:10, 7:11, 7:15, 7:17, 7:21), with Hebrews 7:2–4. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G tag is proposed: in 14:18 Brenton’s Greek agrees with the KJV. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
